name: Hiền Lương Bridge
localName: Cầu Hiền Lương – sông Bến Hải
summary: A bridge over the Bến Hải River, on the 17th parallel, which split Vietnam in two from 1954 to 1975.

hero.alt: The Bến Hải River and Hiền Lương Bridge

eras.title: A temporary line
eras.text: The Geneva Accords of July 1954 divided Vietnam at the 17th parallel, along the Bến Hải River, until elections that were planned for 1956 but never held. The small Hiền Lương Bridge became the border.

eras.label: 1950s–60s
eras.title: A war of flags
eras.text: Each side painted its half of the bridge a different colour and raised ever-taller flagpoles on its bank. Loudspeakers blared propaganda across the water.

image.alt: The flagpole on the north bank

eras.title: Under the bombs
eras.text: The area on both sides of the river became a battlefield. The bridge was destroyed by bombing, and villages north of the river were flattened.

image.file: 17th para taken from N of river.JPG
image.alt: The river seen from the north bank

eras.title: One country
eras.text: With reunification in 1975 the dividing line disappeared. Families separated for twenty years could cross the river again.

eras.label: Today
eras.title: The longing for unity
eras.text: The bridge has been rebuilt in its old form, and the flagpole raised again. A monument on the south bank shows a mother and child longing for reunification.

image.file: Tượng đài Khát vọng thống nhất non sông.JPG

story.title: A river that divided a country
story.narration: When the war against France ended in 1954, the peace agreement signed in Geneva drew a temporary line across Vietnam at the 17th parallel. Troops were to regroup on either side until national elections in 1956. The elections never took place. For twenty-one years the narrow Bến Hải River separated two states, and the Hiền Lương Bridge, under 200 metres long, separated families who could see each other across the water but not meet.

story.title: The mother who mended the flag

image.file: Người mẹ vá cờ Hiền Lương.JPG
image.alt: Statue of the mother mending the flag

story.narration: On the north bank stood a tall flagpole, and on the south bank another. The flags were targets, torn by wind and gunfire. People of the Vĩnh Linh area, many of them women, sewed and mended the northern flag again and again, sometimes at night, so that it would fly every morning. A statue of a mother mending the flag now stands near the bridge. The flagpole on the north bank has been rebuilt, and a large flag flies there today.

story.title: A village underground

image.file: 17th para taken from N of river.JPG
image.alt: The area north of the river

story.narration: North of the river, the village of Vĩnh Mốc was bombed almost every day. Its people dug tunnels about two kilometres long, on three levels, down to more than 20 metres underground. Families lived there for years, with small rooms, wells and a meeting hall. Children were born in the tunnels. Today visitors can walk through them, bending low, and come out at exits facing the sea.

guide.price: Small fee for the exhibition and flagpole area.

hours.notes: Approximate. The bridge itself is always open to walk across.

do: Keep your voice low and dress modestly.
Light incense only where others do so.
Visit the Vĩnh Mốc tunnels, about 15 km away.
dont: Pose playfully for photos at graves and memorials.
Wander off paths in the countryside; old ordnance is still found.

tips.title: Local food
tips.text: Try bánh bột lọc and cháo canh (thick noodle soup) in Đồng Hới and Đông Hà.

tips.title: Getting there
tips.text: About 1.5 hours by road from Huế, or 2 hours from Đồng Hới.

tips.title: Nearby
tips.text: Vĩnh Mốc tunnels, the Quảng Trị citadel, and Phong Nha caves further north.
